header:
Date: 2026-12-10
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Reddy (Redwood SE), Sarah Chen (Aurelius CTO), Mike Alvarez (Aurelius Head of Infra), Liam O'Connor (Aurelius SRE), Dana Flores (Aurelius Security)
Recording: Yes
Notes: Deep dive on Private VPC networking options (PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, DNS) and runtime implications for KV cache, batching, quantization
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, appreciate you making time. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Sarah (Aurelius - CTO): Sarah here.
[00:08] Mike (Aurelius - Infra): Mike on the call.
[00:09] Liam (Aurelius - SRE): Liam here.
[00:11] Dana (Aurelius - Security): Dana here.
[00:13] Maya: Great, and from Redwood we have Jonah and Priya, SEs. Quick agenda — we want to cover networking architecture options for Private VPC deployment: PrivateLink vs VPC peering, NAT considerations, subnets, DNS routing to the control plane, and then go into runtime implications — KV cache placement, batching/throughput impacts, quantization artifacts. Sound ok?
[00:32] Sarah: Yes, that's perfect. We're especially concerned about latency and also the security posture — we can't have any egress to public internet for model inference traffic.
[00:40] Jonah (Redwood SE): Totally, and that's been a common constraint. We'll walk through three patterns: PrivateLink (AWS), VPC peering, and Transit Gateway style. Each has tradeoffs for latency and cross-az traffic.
[00:52] Priya (Redwood SE): Quick note, sometimes the transcript generator writes Private link as two words or PrivateLink as one, you might see both in our docs, sorry.
[00:58] Mike: ha no worries. So, for Aurelius, our requirement is: inference traffic and control plane calls must stay within our VPC, no public egress except for rare management. We also have strict subnets per compliance.
[01:12] Jonah: Understood. For that, PrivateLink is frequently chosen because it creates an ENI in your subnet and traffic stays in the AWS backbone. You get an interface endpoint that talks to Redwood's endpoint service. Latency is usually low, but there's an extra hop through the ENI and NLB.
[01:30] Liam: Do you see any jitter when using PrivateLink across AZs?
[01:34] Jonah: A little. With cross-AZ requests you'll see inter-AZ network cost and slightly higher p95 — like +2 to +6 ms depending on region and AZ topology. If you keep compute and the PrivateLink endpoint in same AZ, it's minimal.
[01:45] Sarah: Ok. What about KV cache behavior? Our workload uses lots of short-turn prompts and we rely on the KV (key-value) cache for prefix reuse. If the cache is not local, that could kill latency.
[01:58] Priya: Great question. Our runtime keeps KV cache in the local serving instance memory. If you host Redwood Private in your VPC (the Private deployment), the KV cache is local to the GPU instance(s). The networking pattern mainly affects control-plane calls (e.g., model manifest, health pings) and streaming RPCs.
[02:15] Mike: So streaming tokens still cross the PrivateLink link?
[02:18] Jonah: Yes, requests and streaming responses go over the interface — but the heavy token generation loops are on the instance in your VPC or Dedicated pool. If you're using Hosted API with PrivateLink, then traffic traverses to Redwood-managed infra; if you're on Redwood Private (customer-hosted in VPC) then the runtime and KV cache are inside your network entirely.
[02:37] Sarah: For our compliance we prefer Redwood Private in our VPC. What are the notes on DNS? We need to resolve service endpoints to the interface endpoint IPs and ensure certs still validate.
[02:50] Maya: For AWS PrivateLink we recommend using the AWS-provided private DNS option for the interface endpoint — that rewrites the service hostname to the private IP, so your existing hostname (api.redwood.example) resolves to the ENI. Certificate validation uses the same public certs; the TLS handshake is end-to-end to Redwood. Sometimes customers prefer to use their own private zone and CNAMEs, but that adds ops complexity.
[03:10] Dana: Is there any leak to public IPs during model downloads or kernel pulls? We run air-gapped-ish environments.
[03:18] Jonah: If you're doing a Private deployment with on-prem or VPC-only, model artifacts can be pulled from a customer-controlled S3 or via signed transfer — Redwood supports pulling over VPC endpoints to avoid public egress. For hosted updates, we'd negotiate a secure CDN location; but we can also do an offline bundle. We do see customers use a staged sync bucket inside the customer's account.
[03:39] Mike: Ok good. Let's talk throughput — we might push spikes to 1k qps for short bursts. How do batching and the runtime affect that in a PrivateLink setup?
[03:50] Jonah: Batching increases efficiency, so for high throughput you want some aggregation at the ingress — Redwood's runtime supports adaptive batching and can batch across concurrent requests on the same instance. The network path (PrivateLink) can carry that traffic fine; the limiting factors are instance GPU throughput and max concurrent streaming connections per NLB. If you have a dedicated pool in your VPC, you can scale instances horizontally and the router will distribute work.
[04:12] Liam: We worry about burst shaping — if hundreds of small requests hit simultaneously, what's the p95?
[04:18] Jonah: We typically see p95 impacted by batch formation time. If you set batch_max_latency to 20ms, you trade off a bit of tail latency for much higher throughput and lower cost per token. In our internal tests, at 1k qps with batching you get much better GPU utilization and average token latency similar to unbatched but lower cost. We'll run a benchmark with your payload to show numbers.
[04:41] Sarah: Sounds good. Any constraints about the ENI quotas or endpoints per VPC?
[04:46] Priya: AWS has limits on interface endpoints per region/VPC and there are NLB connection limits. In practice, most customers create a PrivateLink endpoint per service and use cross-AZ redundancy. We'll share a checklist of required quota increases; that's in the action items.
[04:59] Mike: About NAT — do you need egress via NAT for health checks or logging?
[05:04] Jonah: For hosted control plane you'd need limited egress for metrics/logs to Redwood's telemetry collectors unless you opt into a private telemetry pipeline. But in Redwood Private, logs can be configured to stay in your VPC (CloudWatch, S3) via VPC endpoints — no NAT required. If there's any external call, ensure your NAT has rules for the specific endpoints.
[05:24] Dana: Are the keys always client-managed? We need KMS integration and audit logs.
[05:28] Maya: Yes, for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS. Logs can be pushed to your logging stack and we support audit logging at request granularity. We'll include the SOC2 excerpt and KMS integration notes in the doc pack.
[05:42] Sarah: Great. Can you walk through a sample flow end-to-end — request path, where KV cache lives, where batching happens?
[05:50] Jonah: Sure. Example: client -> PrivateLink interface endpoint in your subnet -> NLB (Redwood side) -> Router -> selected GPU instance (running in your VPC if private) -> runtime checks local KV cache (in-memory on that instance). If cached prefix exists we hit fast path and return tokens quickly. Batching happens at the instance process: incoming requests accumulate in a small queue then the attention kernels are executed on the GPU with combined batch. Responses stream back through the same path.
[06:20] Liam: If the request is routed to a different instance that doesn't have the KV cache, do you have distributed KV?
[06:25] Jonah: We currently do not have a globally shared in-memory KV cache due to consistency/perf tradeoffs. We rely on adaptive routing and sticky sessions to increase cache locality. For cross-instance reuse, we recommend either: 1) pinning certain routes to instances, or 2) using prefix caching on the client side or at an edge caching layer. We can also configure a small warmup/replicate window for hot prefixes.
[06:48] Sarah: So there's a routing policy we can tune?
[06:51] Priya: Yes, you can set routing hints: prefer-local-cache, prefer-latency, or round-robin. For latency-critical workloads prefer-local-cache and smaller autoscale steps so instances keep warm and cache hot prefixes.
[07:05] Mike: Can you quantify the p50/p95 hit if we switch from prefer-latency to prefer-local-cache?
[07:10] Jonah: Roughly, prefer-local-cache improves p95 for cache-hit traffic by 15-30% because you avoid cache-miss cold starts. But if your traffic is highly distributed across users and prefixes, you might see a slight p50 increase for cold requests because we constrain routing. We'll capture exact numbers in the benchmark.
[07:28] Sarah: What about multi-AZ deployment? We require redundancy. If KV is local, how do you handle failover?
[07:35] Jonah: In multi-AZ, instances in each AZ maintain their own local KV caches. The router will detect instance health and re-route; when an instance fails requests go to another AZ, which may have a cold cache and thus higher latency for the first few requests. We mitigate by proactive replication of small hot prefix sets and fast instance warmup routines.
[07:56] Liam: Is cross-AZ replication a background process? What's the consistency model?
[07:59] Priya: It's async replication for warmups, not strong consistency. The goal is to reduce cold-starts for hot prefixes. If you need strong consistency across all copies that's a different design tradeoff that impacts latency and throughput.
[08:12] Mike: Let's talk about monitoring — we need per-token latency and token cost breakdown visible in our console.
[08:18] Maya: Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdown, latency histograms, per-route model metrics. For Private deployments metrics can be shipped to your CloudWatch or Prometheus stack via an agent or VPC endpoint. We'll include sample Grafana dashboards.
[08:31] Dana: Audit logs — what's the retention by default and can we extend?
[08:34] Maya: Default is 90 days for request logs, longer retention is an add-on. For Private deployments you can push logs to your S3 and apply your retention policies.
[08:44] Sarah: One more thing — quantization. We want to run 8-bit quantized models to reduce cost. Any network or runtime caveats for quantized models?
[08:54] Jonah: Quantized models mainly affect CPU/GPU kernel selection and memory footprint. Network-wise no difference. But quantization can change latency characteristics slightly because kernels may run different code paths; we benchmark each quant profile. Also, quantized models can have slightly different token generation timing due to kernel memory access patterns. We'll include quantization-specific perf numbers in the benchmark for your model sizes.
[09:18] Liam: For our use-case we do a lot of short chat-like prompts; quantization seems promising. Will the KV cache hold quantized keys differently?
[09:26] Jonah: KV cache stores activations/kv-values in float16 or int8 depending on runtime config. The runtime will store them in the most efficient format; we maintain compatibility so that cached prefixes serve correctly regardless of quantization, but there are implementation details we'll document.
[09:43] Mike: How about TLS termination — does Redwood terminate at the NLB or at the instance?
[09:48] Priya: We support TLS's end-to-end. For PrivateLink the TLS terminates at the Redwood service endpoint by default; if you want mTLS or client certs, we can configure mutual TLS to the runtime. For Private deployments inside your VPC the TLS is to the instance, and you can use your certs if needed.
[10:05] Sarah: Any pitfalls we should watch for during pilot?
[10:08] Jonah: A few: 1) Subnet IP exhaustion because each interface endpoint uses an IP in the subnet — pick subnets with spare capacity. 2) Make sure route tables and NACLs allow traffic between the ENIs and your instances. 3) ENI quotas and NLB connection limits. 4) DNS caching — some OS-level caches might not pick up private DNS rewrites immediately.
[10:33] Mike: On the IP exhaustion: if we have very small private subnets we might blow through ENI IPs quickly?
[10:39] Priya: Yes, if you create multiple endpoints or autoscale many ENIs per AZ you need to ensure /28 or larger subnets are available for the interface endpoints. We'll include recommended CIDR sizes.
[10:51] Sarah: Let's capture the exact items we need from our side to get a pilot: subnets + route table IDs, expected qps profile, sample payloads, security contact, and whether we want Redwood-managed or customer KMS.
[11:03] Maya: I'll note that down— that's consistent with our next_steps. Jonah, any final runtime items?
[11:07] Jonah: We'll run two benchmarks: 1) local-private-hosted-style with KV locality and batching; 2) cross-AZ with cold cache to show tail. We'll produce p50/p95/p99 for token latency and GPU utilization, plus cost per token. We'll also test quantized vs fp16 variants.
[11:24] Liam: Can you also include connection churn tests to simulate thousands of short-lived TCP streams?
[11:28] Jonah: Yep, we'll add churn tests and NLB capacity notes.
[11:31] Dana: Anything on SSO/SSO provisioning? We need SAML and SCIM for user provisioning for the console.
[11:36] Maya: We support SAML SSO and SCIM; for Private deployments the control plane can link to your IdP. We'll attach docs.
[11:44] Sarah: Ok this has been super helpful. Let's capture a short recap.
[11:49] Maya: Recap: Aurelius prefers Private deployment in VPC, will provide subnets and CIDR, Redwood will run 1k qps-ish benchmarks showing batching/quantization impacts, share PrivateLink checklist, DNS and cert notes, SOC2/KMS docs, and schedule follow-up week of 12/21. Action items are in the doc. Any last comments?
[12:10] Mike: None here.
[12:12] Sarah: Thanks everyone.
[12:13] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with docs and benchmark timeline. Bye.
[12:17] [END]
notes: Meeting recorded; follow-up packet to include architecture diagram, quota checklist, benchmark spreadsheet, SOC2 excerpt, KMS integration notes, and sample Grafana dashboards.
